questions.question: What is "media literacy"?
options: The ability to understand, analyse and critically evaluate media content
The ability to read quickly
Knowing how to publish your own videos
Having accounts on many social media platforms
questions.explanation: Media literacy is the critical skill of understanding, analysing and evaluating media content — essential in a world of misinformation.

questions.question: What is a "filter bubble"?
options: When you only see content that confirms your existing views
A tool that removes spam from your feed
A privacy setting on social media
A type of camera filter
questions.explanation: Algorithms feed you content similar to what you already engage with, so you mainly see things that confirm your existing viewpoints.

questions.question: According to an MIT study, how fast do false news stories spread compared to true ones?
options: About 6 times faster
At the same speed
Slightly slower
Twice as slowly
questions.explanation: The MIT study found that false news spreads about six times faster than true news, partly because it is more sensational.

questions.question: Why do algorithms tend to promote controversial and emotional content?
options: Because it generates more engagement, which keeps users on the platform
Because it is more likely to be true
Because moderators select it manually
Because the law requires platforms to show it
questions.explanation: Algorithms optimise for engagement, not truth — and controversial, emotionally charged content gets more reactions and shares.

questions.question: Which question is most useful for evaluating media content critically?
options: Who made this content, and why?
How many likes does it have?
Is the video in high resolution?
How long is the article?
questions.explanation: Asking who created the content and what their purpose is reveals possible bias — likes and length say nothing about reliability.
